claims.text: Spin-polarized DFT can reliably determine the presence of ferromagnetic ground states in transition-metal systems.
Ferromagnetic ground states can be identified by comparing the total energies of spin-polarized and spin-unpolarized configurations.
The proposed material is a transition-metal-based material containing elements with magnetic d electrons.
The material begins in a metastable disordered or high-temperature state.
The method requires one calculation that permits magnetic ordering and another constrained to a nonmagnetic solution.
The calculations should be performed at 0 K or at a sufficiently low temperature that thermal effects are minimal.
Strongly correlated systems may require inclusion of a Hubbard U term.
Atomic arrangements and local chemical environments produce electronic exchange splitting.
Spin-polarized DFT captures exchange-correlation energy differences between magnetic and nonmagnetic configurations.
A lower total energy for a configuration with a net magnetic moment indicates a ferromagnetic ground state.
Energy lowering relative to the nonmagnetic solution demonstrates that the electronic structure favors ferromagnetic ordering.
A spin-polarized state that has lower energy and nonzero net magnetization predicts a ferromagnetic ground state.
A lower-energy spin-unpolarized state indicates the absence of ferromagnetism.
A spin-unpolarized DFT calculation assumes no magnetic ordering and returns zero net magnetization.
The method is most reliable when DFT adequately describes electronic exchange and correlation.
Very strong electronic correlations or significant relativistic effects may require more advanced treatments.
Predicted energy differences and magnetic moments may depend on the exchange-correlation functional.
Changes in composition or microstructure may alter the predicted ferromagnetic character.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome treats a lower-energy nonmagnetic state as a valid negative diagnosis of ferromagnetism, whereas the falsification rule treats that same result as falsifying the proposed detection hypothesis for the material.
